claim: Hmga1 is highly expressed prior to neural crest specification and maintained in migrating chick neural crest cells.
source: Using single-cell RNA sequencing coupled with high-resolution in situ hybridization to identify novel transcriptional regulators, we show that chromatin remodeler Hmga1 is highly expressed prior to specification and maintained in migrating chick neural crest cells.
evidence: The abstract directly states this finding based on scRNA-seq and in situ hybridization experiments described in the manuscript.

claim: At the neural plate border, Hmga1 regulates Pax7-dependent neural crest lineage specification.
source: At the neural plate border, Hmga1 regulates Pax7-dependent neural crest lineage specification.
evidence: This claim is supported by CRISPR-Cas9 knockout experiments showing loss of Pax7 expression and rescue experiments with Pax7 overexpression.

claim: At premigratory stages, Hmga1 loss reduces cranial crest emigration from the dorsal neural tube independent of Pax7.
source: At premigratory stages, a second role manifests where Hmga1 loss reduces cranial crest emigration from the dorsal neural tube independent of Pax7.
evidence: Temporally controlled knockouts showed migration defects without affecting Pax7 expression when Hmga1 was lost after specification.

claim: Hmga1 emigration defects are rescued by stabilized β-catenin, implicating Hmga1 as a canonical Wnt activator.
source: Interestingly, this is rescued by stabilized ß-catenin, thus implicating Hmga1 as a canonical Wnt activator.
evidence: Rescue experiments with stabilized β-catenin restored migration defects caused by Hmga1 loss.

claim: Neural crest cells originate at the neural plate border.
source: Originating at the neural plate border, these cells occupy the leading edges of the closing neural folds during neurulation.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the neural crest field.

claim: Neural crest cells undergo epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition to delaminate and migrate.
source: Subsequently, premigratory neural crest cells that initially reside within the dorsal aspect of the developing neural tube undergo an epithelial-to-mesenchymal (EMT) transition in order to delaminate and migrate extensively.
evidence: This is well-established knowledge about neural crest development.

claim: Neural crest cells differentiate into craniofacial cartilage, pigment cells, smooth muscle, and peripheral neurons and glia.
source: Upon reaching their terminal locations within the embryo, neural crest cells differentiate into a plethora of derivatives, including craniofacial cartilage, pigment cells, smooth muscle, and peripheral neurons and glia (reviewed in Gandhi and Bronner, 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a review article.

claim: A feed-forward gene regulatory network underlies neural crest formation from induction to differentiation.
source: A feed-forward gene regulatory network (GRN) underlies the formation of the neural crest, from induction at the neural plate border to final differentiation into a multitude of cell types.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field, supported by citations.

claim: The neural crest GRN is comprised of transcription factors and signaling pathways partitioned into developmental modules.
source: This GRN is comprised of transcription factors and signaling pathways, partitioned into developmental modules (Martik and Bronner, 2017; Simões-Costa et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Single-cell RNA sequencing and ATAC-seq have enabled analysis of the neural crest GRN at a global level.
source: Recently, new tools like single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) and Assay for Transposase-Accessible Chromatin using sequencing (ATAC-seq) have enabled analysis of the neural crest GRN at a global level, helping to clarify lineage trajectories and elucidate key biological processes therein, ranging from proliferation to differentiation (Williams et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Williams et al., 2019.

claim: Gastrula stage chick embryos show high overlap of multiple transcription factors in single cells in the neural plate border region.
source: Quantitative gene expression analysis of gastrula stage chick embryos has revealed a surprisingly high degree of overlap of multiple transcription factors associated with diverse cell types within single cells in the early neural plate border region, ranging from markers characteristic of the neural crest (Pax7), to neural (Sox2) and placodal (Six1) cell types (Roellig et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Roellig et al., 2017.

claim: Cells in the neural plate border are transcriptionally primed toward multiple cell fates rather than committed to a particular lineage.
source: This is consistent with the possibility that cells in the neural plate border are transcriptionally primed toward multiple cell fates, rather than committed to a particular lineage.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation of overlapping transcription factor expression.

claim: Hmga1 is a non-histone chromatin remodeler with known roles in tumor metastasis.
source: One of the genes uncovered in the neural crest cluster was Hmga1, a non-histone chromatin remodeler that has known roles in tumor metastasis (Resar et al., 2018), but has been understudied in development.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Resar et al., 2018.

claim: Hmga1 transcripts are enriched in the neural crest with onset of expression preceding neural crest specification in the neural plate border.
source: We first characterized the expression and function of Hmga1 during neural crest development using in situ Hybridization Chain Reaction (HCR) and observed Hmga1 transcripts enriched in the neural crest, with the onset of expression preceding neural crest specification in the neural plate border.
evidence: This is based on HCR data shown in the manuscript.

claim: Loss of Hmga1 results in downregulation of neural crest specifier genes Snail2, FoxD3, and Sox10.
source: The results demonstrate an early role for Hmga1 in neural crest lineage specification in a Pax7-dependent manner, resulting in the downregulation of neural crest specifier genes such as Snail2, FoxD3, and Sox10.
evidence: This is based on in situ hybridization and immunohistochemistry data in the manuscript.

claim: Loss of Hmga1 after neural crest specification reveals defects in cranial neural crest emigration and migration.
source: Interestingly, loss of Hmga1 after completion of neural crest specification revealed a distinct set of defects in cranial neural crest emigration and migration.
evidence: This is based on temporally controlled CRISPR experiments described in the manuscript.

claim: Hmga1 regulates canonical Wnt activity mediated by Wnt1 in delaminating neural crest cells.
source: Using in situ hybridization and a fluorescent protein-based reporter, we show that this is a consequence of reduced canonical Wnt activity mediated by Wnt1, which can be rescued by concomitantly expressing stabilized ß-catenin, thus establishing a separate role for Hmga1 in delaminating neural crest cells as a Wnt pathway activator.
evidence: This is based on Wnt reporter assays, in situ hybridization for Wnt1, and rescue experiments with stabilized β-catenin.

claim: The single-cell RNA-seq profiled 1268 cells, of which 1241 passed quality control filters.
source: The library was sequenced at a depth of 50,000 median reads/cell to profile a total of 1268 cells, out of which 1241 cells passed the quality control filters (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–C).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the scRNA-seq data.

claim: Dimensional reduction using UMAP identifies six subpopulations in the dissociated embryonic hindbrain.
source: Dimensional reduction using UMAP identifies six subpopulations (including the spike-in) contained within the dissociated embryonic hindbrain.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1B and described in the text.

claim: The neural crest subcluster is distinguished by enrichment of Tfap2B and ItgB3 markers.
source: Known genetic markers that were enriched in each population served to distinguish the neural crest subcluster (Tfap2B+, ItgB3+) from the surrounding tissues (i.e. otic placode (Cldn3+, Gbx2+); hindbrain (Pax6+, Zic2+); ectoderm (Epcam+, Crabp2+); mesoderm (FoxC2+, Col1A1+)) (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A–B).
evidence: This is based on marker gene expression analysis in the scRNA-seq data.

claim: Hmga1 is a member of the High Motility Group A (HMGA) superfamily that binds to the minor groove of DNA.
source: A member of the High Motility Group A (HMGA) superfamily, Hmga1 encodes a small, nonhistone chromatin remodeling protein that binds to the minor groove of DNA, thereby affecting the chromatin landscape and facilitating the binding of other transcription factors in the opposing major groove (Grosschedl et al., 1994).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: In developing mouse embryos, Hmga1 has widespread expression across several tissues including the brain.
source: In developing mouse embryos, Hmga1 has been shown to have widespread expression across several tissues, including the brain, where its loss has been correlated with reduced developmental potential of neural precursor cells (Kishi et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Kishi et al., 2012.

claim: Loss of Hmga1 in mouse brain has been correlated with reduced developmental potential of neural precursor cells.
source: In developing mouse embryos, Hmga1 has been shown to have widespread expression across several tissues, including the brain, where its loss has been correlated with reduced developmental potential of neural precursor cells (Kishi et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Kishi et al., 2012.

claim: Hmga1 transcripts were first detected in the neural plate and neural plate border at HH4+, preceding Pax7 expression.
source: Hmga1 transcripts were first detected in the neural plate and neural plate border, but not in the non-neural ectoderm at HH4+, and preceded the expression of Pax7 in the neural plate border.
evidence: This is based on HCR data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Hmga1 expression overlaps with Pax7 in the neural plate border at HH5-6.
source: Hmga1 expression remained high at HH5-6 (Figure 2A–B), overlapping in the neural plate border (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A) with Pax7 transcripts (Figure 2B'), as observed in transverse sections (Figure 2B", Figure 2—figure supplement 1B–B').
evidence: This is based on HCR data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Hmga1 expression is retained in the neural tube as neural folds elevate between HH7 and HH8.
source: As the neural plate border elevated to form neural folds between HH7 and HH8 (Figure 2D'''), expression of Hmga1 was retained in the neural tube (Figure 2C–D) and continued to overlap with Pax7 in the dorsal neural folds (Figure 2D', Figure 2—figure supplement 1C–D').
evidence: This is based on HCR data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Hmga1 is expressed in both leader and follower cells within the migrating neural crest stream at HH10.
source: Interestingly, transverse sections through a representative HH10 embryo revealed that within the migrating neural crest stream, Hmga1 was expressed in both leader and follower cells, as compared to Pax7, which appeared to be downregulated in the leader cells (Figure 2F'').
evidence: This is based on HCR data shown in Figure 2F''.

claim: Electroporation of Cas9 and Hmga1 gRNAs resulted in loss of Hmga1 transcripts in the neural crest.
source: Electroporation of Cas9 and Hmga1 gRNAs on the right side resulted in loss of Hmga1 transcripts in the neural crest as confirmed using HCR.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3C and quantified in Figure 3D.

claim: Hmga1 knockout results in a 25% reduction in Hmga1 expression in whole-mount embryos.
source: We quantified this phenotype in whole-mount embryos and observed a 25% reduction in Hmga1 expression (Figure 3D, Figure 3—source data 1; p<0.05, Wilcoxon rank test).
evidence: This is based on quantification of HCR data.

claim: Loss of Hmga1 resulted in a notable reduction in Pax7 mRNA levels.
source: Consistent with their hierarchical onset of expression, loss of Hmga1 resulted in a notable reduction in Pax7 mRNA levels (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3E using HCR.

claim: Hmga1 knockout resulted in a significant decrease in the number of Pax7+ cells.
source: As expected, Pax7 protein levels were dramatically reduced in the migratory cranial neural crest (Figure 3F,H'), with further analysis revealing a significant decrease in the number of Pax7+ cells on the knockout side compared to the control side (Figure 3G, Figure 3—source data 2; p<0.0001, student's t-test).
evidence: This is based on immunostaining and cell counting data.

claim: In the absence of Hmga1, cranial neural crest cells failed to migrate properly as shown by HNK1 expression.
source: Moreover, in the absence of Hmga1, cranial neural crest cells failed to migrate properly, as depicted by the expression of the migratory neural crest marker HNK1 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Neural crest specifier genes FoxD3, Tfap2b, Sox10, and c-Myc were downregulated following Hmga1 knockout.
source: Furthermore, using in situ hybridization, we found that other neural crest specifier genes including FoxD3 (Figure 3J,J', Figure 3—figure supplement 1D,E',E''), Tfap2b (Figure 3K), Sox10 (Figure 3L,L'), and c-Myc (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C) were also downregulated on the knockout side.
evidence: This is based on in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 3.

claim: No notable difference in neural tube thickness was observed following Hmga1 knockout.
source: On the other hand, no notable difference in the thickness of the neural tube was observed (Figure 3H,J',M'', Figure 3—figure supplement 1E), suggesting that the targeted knockout of Hmga1 in the neural plate border affected the neural folds/dorsal neural tube but not the neural plate itself.
evidence: This is based on analysis of sections shown in Figure 3.

claim: The ratio of Pax7+ cells between experimental and control sides is significantly different between midbrain and hindbrain levels.
source: Accordingly, we noticed that while this ratio was 0.948 ± 0.036 (n = 5) at the midbrain level, it was significantly reduced in the dorsal hindbrain, with a mean ratio of 0.69 ± 0.08 (n = 5; p<0.05, paired Student's t-test) (Figure 4C, Figure 4—source data 1).
evidence: This is based on quantification of Pax7+ cells in sections.

claim: Cas9-protein-mediated loss of Hmga1 resulted in downregulation of Pax7 expression in the neural plate border.
source: Cas9-protein-mediated loss of Hmga1 resulted in downregulation of Pax7 expression in the neural plate border on the right side (experimental side; arrowhead).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4F and quantified in Figure 4J.

claim: The Pax7 fluorescence intensity was significantly reduced on the Hmga1 knockout side compared to control.
source: We also quantified the corrected Pax7 total fluorescence intensity (C.T.C.F) in the neural plate border and observed a statistically significant difference between the control and knockout sides (p<0.01, paired student's t-test), with mean Pax7 intensity on the control side being 89.853 ± 23.388 a.u. (n = 5) as compared to 42.763 ± 16.079 a.u. (n = 5) on the knockout side (Figure 4J, Figure 4—figure supplement 1H, Figure 4—source data 2).
evidence: This is based on quantification of immunofluorescence data.

claim: Loss of Hmga1 did not affect the rate of cell proliferation or apoptosis in the neural plate border.
source: Transverse sections through the experimental compared with control sides revealed that neural plate border cells no longer expressed Pax7 after the loss of Hmga1 (Figure 4H,I), and that this was not a result of premature apoptosis or aberrant cell proliferation (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B–G', Figure 4—figure supplement 1—source data 1).
evidence: This is based on immunostaining for cleaved-caspase-3 and phospho-histone H3.

claim: Hmga1 knockout caused reduced Pax7 mRNA levels but retained Tfap2a and Msx1 expression.
source: Consistent with the loss of Pax7 protein in the neural plate border, Hmga1 knockout caused reduced Pax7 mRNA levels on the experimental (Figure 4M,P) compared to the control (Figure 4L,O) sides. However, the expression of Tfap2a (Figure 4L',M') and Msx1 (Figure 4O',P') was retained in the absence of Hmga1, together with no noticeable difference in the thickness of the neural plate border (Figure 4L'',M'',O'',P'').
evidence: This is based on HCR data shown in Figure 4.

claim: The mean calculated ratio of Pax7 fluorescence intensity between experimental and control sides was 0.552 ± 0.06, which was statistically significant.
source: However, for Pax7, the mean calculated ratio was 0.552 ± 0.06 (n = 6), with a statistically significant difference between the experimental and control sides (p<0.001, paired Student's t-test).
evidence: This is based on quantification of HCR data.

claim: The mean calculated ratio of Msx1 fluorescence intensity between experimental and control sides was 0.809 ± 0.098, which was not statistically significant.
source: On the other hand, while the mean calculated ratio for Msx1 was 0.809 ± 0.098 (n = 3), the fluorescence intensities were not significantly different between the two sides (Figure 4Q, Figure 4—source data 3).
evidence: This is based on quantification of HCR data.

claim: Overexpression of Hmga1 resulted in a notable reduction in Pax7 expression.
source: The results show that, rather than having the opposite effect to loss of function, overexpression of Hmga1 also resulted in a notable reduction in Pax7 expression on the experimental side (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Maintaining appropriate levels of Hmga1 is critical for proper neural crest specification.
source: This suggests that maintaining appropriate levels of Hmga1 is critical for proper neural crest specification.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that both loss and overexpression of Hmga1 reduce Pax7 expression.

claim: Overexpression of Hmga1 in an Hmga1-knockout background successfully rescued Pax7 levels in cranial neural crest cells.
source: Embryos cultured to HH9+ and immunostained for Pax7 revealed that overexpression of Hmga1 concomitant with knocking out the endogenous gene successfully rescued Pax7 levels in cranial neural crest cells (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5D and quantified in Figure 5E.

claim: The mean ratio of Pax7+ cells in the 'knockout' group was 0.767 ± 0.041, significantly different from the 'rescue' group ratio of 0.946 ± 0.016.
source: In unperturbed embryos, this ratio will be close to 1, reflecting similar numbers of Pax7+ cells on both sides of the embryo. However, in the 'knockout' group, we observed a mean ratio of 0.767 ± 0.041 (n = 11), which was significantly different from the ratio of 0.946 ± 0.016 (n = 8) observed in the 'rescue' group (p<0.001, Welch two-sample t-test) (Figure 5E, Figure 5—source data 1).
evidence: This is based on quantification of Pax7+ cells.

claim: Restoring Hmga1 levels was sufficient to rescue Sox10 and Pax7 expression in early migrating crest.
source: Indeed, restoring the levels of Hmga1 was sufficient to rescue the expression of Sox10 (Figure 5G') and Pax7 (Figure 5G'') in early migrating crest, and Pax7 in the premigratory crest residing in the dorsal neural tube, as visualized in transverse sections through the embryo.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5G using HCR.

claim: Exogenous expression of Pax7 rescued the expression of Tfap2b and Snai2 in an Hmga1 knockout background.
source: Compared to the Hmga1-knockout embryos in which Tfap2b mRNA (Figure 3K) and Snail2 protein (Figure 3I') levels were notably downregulated, restoring the levels of Pax7 in an Hmga1 knockout background rescued the expression of both Tfap2b (Figure 5J) and Snai2 (Figure 5K) in the dorsal hindbrain.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5J and 5K using HCR.

claim: Wnt1 is prominently expressed in the dorsal neural tube at the onset of neural crest emigration.
source: For example, at the onset of neural crest emigration, Wnt1 is prominently expressed in the dorsal neural tube, where premigratory neural crest cells reside (Simões-Costa et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Simões-Costa et al., 2015.

claim: Snai2 is a critical regulator of EMT that functions downstream of the Wnt signaling pathway.
source: As a result, these cells turn on Snai2, a critical regulator of EMT (Nieto et al., 1994) known to function downstream of the Wnt signaling pathway.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Nieto et al., 1994.

claim: Hmga1 knockout caused a notable reduction in canonical Wnt reporter activity at the midbrain level.
source: Consistent with our hypothesis, the results show that Hmga1 knockout caused a notable reduction in canonical Wnt reporter activity on the knockout side compared to the control side (Figure 6C) at the midbrain level.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6C using a Tcf/Lef:H2B-GFP reporter.

claim: Hmga1 knockout embryos had a neural crest migration defect but no notable difference in the number of Pax7+ cells at the midbrain level.
source: Interestingly, these embryos had a neural crest migration defect (Figure 6—figure supplement 1C–D) but no notable difference in the number of Pax7+ cells between the two sides (Figure 6—figure supplement 1E'), as expected if the Hmga1 knockout occurred after specification was complete; this is consistent with previous work showing that perturbation of canonical Wnt signaling following specification does not affect the number of Pax7+ cells at cranial EMT stages (Hutchins and Bronner, 2018).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1 and is consistent with cited work.

claim: The mean ratio of Wnt reporter activity between knockout and control sides was 0.325 ± 0.082, indicating disrupted Wnt signaling.
source: While this ratio was expected to be one for embryos with unperturbed Wnt signaling on both sides, we observed a mean ratio of 0.325 ± 0.082 (n = 5), suggesting that Wnt activity was disrupted in the absence of Hmga1.
evidence: This is based on quantification of Wnt reporter activity shown in Figure 6D.

claim: A putative Wnt1 enhancer contains an AT-rich domain consistent with Hmga1-binding motifs.
source: Interestingly, we discovered a putative enhancer downstream of Wnt1 (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A) that contained an AT-rich domain consistent with Hmga1-binding motifs (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B; Reeves and Nissen, 1990).
evidence: This is based on analysis of ATAC-seq data and sequence analysis, with citation to Reeves and Nissen, 1990.

claim: Dorsal neural tube expression of Wnt1 was severely downregulated in the midbrain following Hmga1 knockout.
source: Indeed, the dorsal neural tube expression of Wnt1 was severely downregulated (Figure 6E) in the midbrain.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6E using in situ hybridization.

claim: No change in Wnt1 expression was observed at the hindbrain level following Hmga1 knockout.
source: In contrast, no change in Wnt1 expression was observed at the hindbrain level (Figure 6F) which, being developmentally 'younger,' instead exhibited a specification defect that resulted in fewer Pax7+ cells in the dorsal neural tube on the experimental side compared to the control side (Figure 6F').
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6F using in situ hybridization.

claim: Hmga1 knockout resulted in defects in basement membrane remodeling and laminin channel formation at midbrain levels.
source: Interestingly, following Hmga1 knockout, we also observed defects in basement membrane remodeling and laminin channel formation at midbrain levels (Figure 6G), another Wnt-dependent process necessary for neural crest EMT; consistent with Wnt inhibition via Draxin overexpression (Hutchins and Bronner, 2019), loss of Hmga1 abrogated laminin remodeling and resulted in physical blockage of the channel through which migrating cranial neural crest cells normally transit (Figure 6H).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6G-H using laminin immunostaining, with citation to Hutchins and Bronner, 2019.

claim: Expression of stabilized β-catenin was sufficient to rescue proper cranial neural crest migration from Hmga1 knockdown.
source: Consistent with our hypothesis that Hmga1 functions as a Wnt activator in neural crest cells, expression of stabilized ß-catenin was sufficient to rescue proper cranial neural crest migration from Hmga1 knockdown (Figure 6J).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6J.

claim: After Hmga1 loss, the ratio of migration areas on experimental versus control sides was 0.642 ± 0.028.
source: However, after the loss of Hmga1, the ratio of areas on experimental versus control sides was 0.642 ± 0.028 (n = 5).
evidence: This is based on quantification of migration area shown in Figure 6K.

claim: Co-expression of stabilized β-catenin in premigratory neural crest rescued migration with an average ratio of 1.015 ± 0.035, significantly different from the knockout group.
source: Importantly, co-expression of stabilized ß-catenin in premigratory neural crest rescued migration, with an average migration ratio of 1.015 ± 0.035 (n = 4), which was significantly different from the knockout group (p<0.0001, ANOVA and post hoc Tukey HSD).
evidence: This is based on quantification of migration area shown in Figure 6K.

claim: Ubiquitous expression of Hmga1 coding sequence rescued neural crest migration with an average ratio of 0.972 ± 0.044, significantly different from the knockout group.
source: Similarly, ubiquitous expression of the Hmga1 coding sequence also rescued neural crest migration, with an average migration ratio of 0.972 ± 0.044 (n = 5), which was also significantly different from the knockout group (p<0.001, ANOVA and post hoc Tukey HSD).
evidence: This is based on quantification of migration area shown in Figure 6K.

claim: Chromatin modifiers influence gene expression and cell fate decisions at many stages of development.
source: While chromatin modifiers are known to influence gene expression and cell fate decisions at many stages of development (Cai et al., 2014; Laugesen and Helin, 2014; Miller and Hendrich, 2018; O'Shaughnessy-Kirwan et al., 2015), parsing cell-type-specific functions and targets for these proteins is often challenging due to broad expression across multiple tissues and time points.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: Canonical Wnt signaling is a major input in the neural crest GRN that controls specification and cell lineage decisions.
source: The canonical Wnt signaling pathway is a major input in a complex GRN that activates transcriptional circuits and controls neural crest specification and cell lineage decisions (Martik and Bronner, 2017; Simões-Costa and Bronner, 2015; Williams et al., 2019), influencing multiple aspects of neural crest development from induction at the neural plate border to proliferation, onset of migration via EMT, and differentiation (Milet and Monsoro-Burq, 2012; Rabadán et al., 2016; Simões-Costa and Bronner, 2015; Steventon et al., 2009; Wu et al., 2003; Yanfeng et al., 2003).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: Regulation of canonical Wnt signaling levels is critical for progressive basement membrane remodeling during neural tube closure and neural crest delamination.
source: For example, regulation of the levels of canonical Wnt signaling is critical for progressive basement membrane remodeling during neural tube closure and neural crest delamination. Consequently, perturbation of Wnt signaling output at different stages of basement membrane remodeling or delamination causes severe defects in neural crest EMT (Hutchins and Bronner, 2019; Rabadán et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Hutchins and Bronner, 2019 and Rabadán et al., 2016.

claim: Early inhibition of canonical Wnt signaling in gastrula stage chick embryos reduces Pax7 expression.
source: Interestingly, early inhibition of canonical Wnt signaling in gastrula stage chick embryos has been shown to reduce Pax7 expression (Basch et al., 2006), whereas canonical Wnt inhibition after neural crest specification does not alter Pax7 expression but has a marked effect on EMT (Hutchins and Bronner, 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Basch et al., 2006 and Hutchins and Bronner, 2018.

claim: Canonical Wnt inhibition after neural crest specification does not alter Pax7 expression but has a marked effect on EMT.
source: Interestingly, early inhibition of canonical Wnt signaling in gastrula stage chick embryos has been shown to reduce Pax7 expression (Basch et al., 2006), whereas canonical Wnt inhibition after neural crest specification does not alter Pax7 expression but has a marked effect on EMT (Hutchins and Bronner, 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Hutchins and Bronner, 2018.

claim: Hmga1 has been shown to upregulate canonical Wnt signaling components and downstream targets in the intestinal stem cell niche.
source: Hmga1 has been shown to upregulate canonical Wnt signaling components and downstream targets in the intestinal stem cell niche, thereby amplifying signaling output (Xian et al., 2017) presumably through increased promotor accessibility.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Xian et al., 2017.

claim: Loss of Hmga1 reduced Wnt1 expression following completion of neural crest specification, but not at earlier stages of neural crest induction.
source: However, temporally controlled knockdowns revealed that loss of Hmga1 reduced Wnt1 expression following completion of neural crest specification, but not at earlier stages of neural crest induction.
evidence: This is based on in situ hybridization data at different developmental stages.

claim: Hmga1 knockdown affected Pax7 expression during neural crest induction but not after specification is complete.
source: Conversely, Hmga1 knockdown affected Pax7 expression during neural crest induction but not after specification is complete.
evidence: This is based on temporally controlled knockout experiments.

claim: Neural crest cells exhibit stem-cell-like properties, including multipotency and self-renewal.
source: Neural crest cells exhibit stem-cell-like properties, including multipotency and self-renewal.
evidence: This is established knowledge about neural crest cells.

claim: Hmga1 has a reported role in maintaining stemness and self-renewal properties in various stem cell and cancer systems.
source: Thus, the early expression of Hmga1 in neural crest precursors, together with its reported role in maintaining stemness and self-renewal properties in various stem cell and cancer systems (Battista et al., 2003; Schuldenfrei et al., 2011; Shah and Resar, 2012), may indicate a role in maintaining neural crest stemness.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Battista et al., 2003; Schuldenfrei et al., 2011; Shah and Resar, 2012.

claim: Self-renewal within the premigratory neural crest is driven by the transcription factor c-Myc.
source: In the dorsal neural tube, self-renewal within the premigratory neural crest is driven by the transcription factor c-Myc (Kerosuo and Bronner, 2016), which together with its binding partner regulates cell cycle progression.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Kerosuo and Bronner, 2016.

claim: The mRNA expression of c-Myc is downregulated in the dorsal neural tube following Hmga1 knockout.
source: Consistent with this possibility, we found that the mRNA expression of c-Myc is downregulated in the dorsal neural tube following Hmga1 knockout.
evidence: This is based on in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Hmga1 is a member of the high motility group A (HMGA) family characterized by A/T-hook domains.
source: Hmga1 is a member of the high motility group A (HMGA) family of genes that are characterized by their A/T-hook domains and the ability to transform chromatin architecture to regulate transcription of target genes.
evidence: This is established knowledge about HMGA family proteins.

claim: Two members of the HMGA family, Hmga1 and Hmga2, have been identified in mammals.
source: To date, two members of the HMGA family, Hmga1 and Hmga2, have been identified in mammals (Reeves et al., 2001), each having distinct roles in oncogenesis (Jun et al., 2015; Meyer et al., 2007; Miyazawa et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Reeves et al., 2001; Jun et al., 2015; Meyer et al., 2007; Miyazawa et al., 2004.

claim: Hmga1/Hmga2 double knockout mice have severe embryonic lethality, compared to less-penetrant effects in individual knockouts.
source: Indeed, Hmga1/Hmga2 double knockout mice have severe embryonic lethality, compared to less-penetrant effects in individual knockouts (Federico et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Federico et al., 2014.

claim: A significant proportion of neural crest cells express Hmga1 but not Hmga2 in chick embryos.
source: While both Hmga1 and Hmga2 genes are annotated in the chick genome, our scRNA-seq results show that a significant proportion of neural crest cells express Hmga1 but not Hmga2.
evidence: This is based on scRNA-seq data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Only the hmga2 paralogue is present in Xenopus laevis embryos.
source: Interestingly, only the hmga2 paralogue is present in Xenopus laevis embryos (Macrì et al., 2016), but morpholino-mediated knockdown of hmga2 did not affect the expression of neural plate border gene pax3/7.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Macrì et al., 2016.

claim: Morpholino-mediated knockdown of hmga2 in Xenopus did not affect the expression of neural plate border gene pax3/7.
source: Interestingly, only the hmga2 paralogue is present in Xenopus laevis embryos (Macrì et al., 2016), but morpholino-mediated knockdown of hmga2 did not affect the expression of neural plate border gene pax3/7.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Macrì et al., 2016.

claim: CHD7 and KDM4A are chromatin remodeling proteins necessary for expression of neural crest specifier genes.
source: For example, both the ATP-dependent chromatin remodeler CHD7 and the histone demethylase Jumonji D2A (KDM4A/JmjD2A) are necessary for expression of neural crest specifier genes; notably, however, these chromatin modifiers appear to function at later developmental time points than Hmga1, as neither knockdown of KDM4A in chick embryos nor CHD7 in Xenopus embryos affect Pax3/7 expression levels (Bajpai et al., 2010; Strobl-Mazzulla et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Bajpai et al., 2010 and Strobl-Mazzulla et al., 2010.

claim: Neither knockdown of KDM4A in chick embryos nor CHD7 in Xenopus embryos affect Pax3/7 expression levels.

claim: KDM4A influences Snai2 and Wnt1 levels.
source: Furthermore, KDM4A influences Snai2 and Wnt1 levels, raising the possibility that Hmga1 may act in concert with KDM4A or other chromatin remodelers to restructure the accessibility of neural crest GRN circuits at different cell fate checkpoints.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and suggests a possible mechanism.

claim: Neural-crest-derived cells are prone to metastasis and give rise to numerous cancers.
source: Post-embryonically, neural-crest-derived cells are prone to metastasis and give rise to numerous cancers (Maguire et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Maguire et al., 2015.

claim: Neural crest and cancer cells often employ similar mechanisms to drive EMT.
source: Furthermore, neural crest and cancer cells often employ similar mechanisms to drive EMT; in particular, the hallmarks of metastasis often involve disruption of the basement membrane which may also be driven by canonical Wnt signaling (Gallik et al., 2017; Powell et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Gallik et al., 2017 and Powell et al., 2013.

claim: High expression levels of Hmga1 have been associated with premature EMT and prolonged stemness in several cancers.
source: Interestingly, high expression levels of Hmga1 have been associated with premature EMT and prolonged stemness in several cancers of the pancreas (Abe et al., 2000), breast (Flohr et al., 2003), lung (Sarhadi et al., 2006), and ovaries (Masciullo et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Abe et al., 2000; Flohr et al., 2003; Sarhadi et al., 2006; Masciullo et al., 2003.
